summary: Lays out the message exchange between two Network Control Programs needed to carry out the Initial Connection Protocol in RFC 123. It shows the server and user sides step by step. It was replaced by RFC 145, which corrected an error in it.

eli5.summary: Two people on a phone call each write down exactly which words they say, one after another. This note is that script for starting a computer connection.

subtitle: J. Postel's April 1971 step-by-step reading of the NCP message exchange behind the Initial Connection Protocol.

tldr.problem: RFC 123 described the Initial Connection Protocol, but it was not spelled out what messages the two Network Control Programs must exchange to carry it out.
tldr.mechanism: The note lays out the server and user NCP steps side by side: request-to-send, send 32 bits, close, then a pair of new connections and allocations.
tldr.outcome: This is one author's interpretation of RFC 123. It was updated by RFC 151 and replaced by RFC 145.

today: This note updates RFC 123, was updated by RFC 151, and was replaced by RFC 145. It is a historical working note from April 1971.

sections.title: An Interpretation of RFC 123
sections.content:
J. Postel of UCLA offers his interpretation of the exchange between Network Control Programs (NCPs) needed to carry out the Initial Connection Protocol of RFC 123. The document is marked as updating RFC 123.

It is a single two-column table, one column for the server NCP and one for the user NCP. All symbols not explained on the page are defined in RFC 123.
sections.eli5: One person's idea of the exact lines each side says when two computers first connect.

sections.title: The Message Exchange
sections.content:
The server NCP listens for a connection on L. The user NCP sends RTS, U, L, l, and the server replies STR, L, U, 32. The server then sends 32 bits of data in one message on a link, with value S, and the user receives it.

Both sides then send a CLS. After that the server sends STR, S+1, U, B and RTS, S, U+1, l, while the user sends STR, U+1, S, B and RTS, U, S+1, l. Each side waits for the connection, sends an ALL, and data then flows on the links.

The note closes by explaining that the l, m and b symbols with subscripts are links, message allocations and bit allocations.
sections.eli5: First one side knocks, the other sends back a number, and they hang up. Then each uses that number to call the other back on two new lines, and they can finally talk.

sections.title: Where It Fits
sections.content:
The note carries no discussion of design or security. It exists to make the ICP of RFC 123 concrete as a sequence of NCP commands. The metadata lists it as updated by RFC 151 and replaced by RFC 145.

For the commands named here (RTS, STR, CLS, ALL), consult the RFC 123 symbols the page refers to rather than this table alone.
sections.eli5: It is a script, not a rule book. Later notes fixed it up.
